content: In December 2013, the first Guideline Development Group (GDG) meeting was convened to identify and agree upon the key PICO (Population, Intervention, Comparator, Outcome) questions that would serve as the foundation for systematic reviews and recommendations. Following this meeting, a survey of GDG members was conducted to prioritize the questions and outcomes based on their clinical relevance and importance. The PICO questions focused on syphilis screening for pregnant women, including options such as no screening, mass treatment, and various test strategies using different diagnostic tests. Only outcomes deemed critical or important to patients and decision-making were included, such as treatment rates (overand under-treatment), cost per case detected, cost per woman screened, screening coverage, side effects, adverse events related to medications and penicillin, accessibility, partner notification and treatment, maternal treatment completion before delivery, maternal complications, and infant outcomes. Systematic reviews for each priority question were conducted by McMaster University, a WHO Collaborating Centre for Evidence-Informed Policy. These reviews examined evidence on desirable and undesirable outcomes, patient values and preferences, resource use, acceptability, equity, and feasibility, drawing from both published and unpublished literature. Comprehensive searches for systematic reviews, randomized controlled trials, and non-randomized studies were performed up to October 2016. Due to limited direct comparative data on screening versus no screening or between different test strategies, cost-effectiveness modeling studies were utilized to provide evidence. For the question comparing screening to no screening, data from a previously published cost-effectiveness analysis were used, presenting infant outcomes. For the question comparing different test strategies, evidence was modeled using diagnostic test accuracy data and calculated effects on important patient outcomes. Cost-effectiveness analyses incorporated field data on syphilis screening and treatment rates in lowand high-prevalence settings, as well as data on the sensitivity and specificity of single rapid syphilis tests (RSTs) and treatment effects. The data were confirmed using an unpublished systematic review of test accuracy data for single RSTs. Outputs of the cost-effectiveness analysis were presented by test strategy and outcomes, including screening rate, treatment rate, missed cases, over-treatment, and cases treated. The evidence for syphilis treatment in pregnant women is detailed in the WHO guidelines for the treatment of Treponema pallidum (syphilis). The quality and certainty of the evidence were assessed using the GRADE (Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation) approach. Evidence quality was categorized into four levels: high, moderate, low, and very low, based on confidence in the effect estimates. Direct costs of medicines were estimated using the 2014 edition of the Management Sciences for Health (MSH) International Drug Price Indicator Guide. All evidence was summarized in GRADE evidence profiles and evidence-to-decision frameworks. During a second GDG meeting in October 2015, the evidence was presented and discussed. The meeting was co-chaired by experts in GRADE methodology and clinical STI management. Additional information was deemed necessary, and screening recommendations were finalized through subsequent teleconferences and electronic communications with the GDG working group for syphilis. The group considered the desirable and undesirable effects of interventions, the value placed on outcomes, associated costs and resource use, acceptability to stakeholders, impact on health equity, and feasibility of implementation. Judgments were made for each criterion, and the strength of each recommendation was determined. Consensus was reached without the need for voting. The finalized recommendations were approved electronically by all GDG members, written up in full, and peer-reviewed. The External Review Group approved the methods and recommendations. Recommendations were rated as either strong or conditional, with strong recommendations using the wording The WHO STI guideline recommends… and conditional recommendations using The WHO STI guideline suggests…. The implications of these recommendations for patients, clinicians, and policymakers were explained in detail. Conflict of interest management was a priority throughout the guideline development process. WHO guidelines for declaration of interests (DOI) were implemented, and DOI statements were obtained from all GDG members before their participation. At the GDG meetings, members disclosed any interests at the start of the meetings. After analyzing each DOI, the WHO STI Secretariat concluded that no member had financial or commercial interests related to STI treatment. Minor interests, such as non-commercial grants or unrelated interests, were noted but did not exclude any member from full participation. The guideline will be disseminated as a printed publication, a downloadable document on the WHO Department of Reproductive Health and Research website, and in the WHO Reproductive Health Library. It will also be available in a guideline application created with GRADEpro GDT software. WHO headquarters will collaborate with regional and country offices to support countries in adapting, implementing, and monitoring the guideline. External partners, including UNFPA, UNICEF, UNAIDS, NGOs, and other agencies, will assist in dissemination and implementation. The guideline will be referenced in other relevant WHO guidelines and presented at major conferences related to STIs and HIV. A system for monitoring new evidence and updating recommendations will be established within a year of guideline implementation. An electronic follow-up survey of key end-users will be conducted after publication to identify challenges, evaluate its usefulness, and address gaps in future editions. The WHO STI guideline strongly recommends screening all pregnant women for syphilis during their first antenatal care visit, based on moderate-quality evidence. This recommendation applies to all settings, regardless of syphilis prevalence. Universal screening is favored over no screening due to significant reductions in adverse pregnancy outcomes and congenital syphilis. It likely increases equity, is cost-effective, and is acceptable to pregnant women and healthcare providers. In settings with low screening coverage, high loss to follow-up, or limited laboratory capacity, the guideline suggests on-site testing strategies over standard off-site laboratory-based screening and treatment.
